headline: High: shared filesystem plus asymmetric write/execute capabilities create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risk in the Copilot–gpt-engineer pair.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot reads repo context and open editor buffers, while gpt-engineer writes files in the project directory and can run a loop that offers to run generated code. That creates a plausible file-based injection path even without clipboard or MCP. The pair lacks explicit provenance tracking, so malicious content in shared files can steer Copilot’s suggestions or gpt-engineer’s prompts.
conditions: IF gpt-engineer writes attacker-controlled instructions into the shared project directory, Copilot may ingest them as repo context.
IF Copilot proposes edits that gpt-engineer later re-reads from files, the instruction payload can persist across turns.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different working copies.
Disable automatic ingestion of newly written files into prompts.
Review generated files before either agent reopens them.
Use a human-approved prompt template for any file-fed context.
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to files and exclude untrusted content from agent context.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot touches source code and open editor buffers, and gpt-engineer reads and writes the user-specified project directory while also handling OPENAI_API_KEY. In a shared workspace, either agent can expose code or secrets into the other’s context, and gpt-engineer’s broad network egress increases the chance of unintended transmission. The pathway exists in default-style use, so this is more than a niche configuration issue.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory, code and buffers can flow between them.
IF gpt-engineer is pointed at a repository containing secrets, its broad egress can transmit those contents to a backend.
mitigations: Remove secrets from the shared project before running either agent.
Use separate repositories or clones per agent.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately after testing.
Restrict gpt-engineer to non-sensitive sample projects.
requires-engineering: enforce redaction before any model upload.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Copilot can write the filesystem and modify git state, while gpt-engineer can write the filesystem, execute shell commands, install packages, and spawn subprocesses. On a shared project directory, both can mutate the same files and one can execute changes the other produced. That overlap is dangerous by default because there is no locking or coordination primitive in either profile.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository, concurrent writes can clobber each other.
IF gpt-engineer executes generated code after Copilot edits the tree, the pair can create inconsistent build or git state.
mitigations: Run only one agent at a time on a given repo.
Use separate branches for each agent.
Pause shell execution in gpt-engineer during collaborative sessions.
Commit or stash before switching agents.
requires-engineering: add file locks or orchestrator-level serialization.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot produces edits for human review, but gpt-engineer’s workflow writes files and can offer to run generated code, so Copilot output can become gpt-engineer input and then executable action. That creates a classic unverified handoff chain. Because gpt-engineer has shell and subprocess authority, a mistaken Copilot suggestion can cascade into real actions or broken project state.
conditions: IF Copilot-generated edits are copied into gpt-engineer prompts, gpt-engineer may treat them as authoritative.
IF gpt-engineer runs code derived from Copilot output, errors can propagate into executed commands or written files.
mitigations: Require human review between agents.
Do not feed raw Copilot output directly into gpt-engineer.
Run gpt-engineer in dry-run mode first.
Verify diffs before any execution step.
requires-engineering: add validation gates before shell execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not declare regulated-data certifications or residency guarantees. The main compliance concern is that gpt-engineer can send project contents to a configured model backend, while Copilot sends context to api.githubcopilot.com. That is a policy mismatch risk, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated-data class like PHI or EU PII, so the blast radius is limited and uncertain.
conditions: IF the project contains regulated data, the two backends may receive it under different vendor policies.
IF an operator requires residency or retention guarantees, the profiles do not document them.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared project.
Check vendor retention settings before use.
Use synthetic data for evaluation.
Review backend destinations before enabling either agent.
requires-engineering: obtain and compare formal compliance attestations.
